Customer: deliver 3 representative client scripts and 48h traffic trace
action_items: Jordan: send runbook + pricing worksheet by 2027-04-20

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-18
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Michaels (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Kestrel Head of ML), Maya Singh (Kestrel SRE), Tomoko Abe (Product), Samir Patel (Infra)

Summary:
Quick scoping for the POC benchmark and harness integration. Focus: validate streaming vs batch for Kestrel's real-time summarization endpoint, define success criteria (latency SLOs + accuracy/regression thresholds), share customer scripts and traffic traces, outline timeline and runbook for a 2-4 week pilot.

Topics covered:
- Workload profile and token distributions
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for their client (mobile + web hybrid)
- SLA and acceptance criteria (p95/p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, cold-start behavior)
- Harness integration details (script formats, auth, telemetry hooks)
- Environment constraints: VPC peering, KMS, SOC2 audit needs
- Logistics and timeline for kickoff and measurement windows

Action items (repeated in metadata above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving time today. quick intro — i'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood side. we were joined by priya and evan. can each of you give a 30 second on roles?
[00:12] Carlos: yeah, hi, Carlos here, head of ML at Kestrel. we're building a live meeting summarization pipeline, need low latency for live captions and a batch re-process for retention.
[00:22] Tomoko: Tomoko, PM. we're measuring user delight plus cost — core metric is real time assistant feel.
[00:28] Maya: maya, SRE. i'll own the network side and peering, and the run-of load shaping during the POC.
[00:34] Jordan: perfect. goal today is to agree on success criteria and the bench harness handoff. quick high-level question: is this mostly real-time streaming or do you have long batch runs too?
[00:44] Carlos: it's both. 60% real time streaming for live calls, 40% non-stream batch for post-call indexing. we expect bursts — like 200 concurrent live sessions at peak but most are small.
[00:58] Priya: got it — when you say 200 concurrent sessions, what's the average tokens-per-second per session? that drives the batching and KV cache behavior.
[01:08] Carlos: average 8 tokens/sec during active speaking; bursts can hit 40 tokens/sec for high-verbosity calls. batch jobs are large: 1.2M tokens over 30-60 minutes.
[01:20] Evan: interesting — that distribution suggests mixing streaming-optimized models for low-latency prefixes and a non-stream quantized variant for batch cost efficiency.
[01:30] Samir: quick infra note: we need to keep data in-region (us-east-1). also we require KMS integration for keys and SOC2 compliance for audit logs.
[01:40] Priya: that's fine — Redwood Private supports VPC with customer KMS; for hosted we can do envelope encryption but for POC we can run in our Dedicated sandbox in us-east.
[01:50] Maya: do you run your dedicated service as a separate VPC or do we peering? security wants peering + strict RBAC.
[01:58] Jordan: we normally do VPC peering for Private; for Dedicated we can do isolated pools within our infra. we'll detail options in the runbook.
[02:08] Tomoko: success criteria — here's what matters to us: p95 latency for streaming < 200ms token response, p99 < 600ms; batch throughput to finish the 1.2M token job within a 45–60 min window; and output fidelity: no more than 3% regression vs our local baseline on summarization ROUGE-like metric.
[02:28] Priya: that's a good starting point. two clarifying items: for streaming p95 are you measuring time-to-first-token or time-to-incremental-chunk?
[02:38] Tomoko: time-to-first-token for user perceived latency, but we also care about steady-state token latency for tail behaviors.
[02:46] Priya: okay we'll instrument both. we'll also capture cold-starts — tail latency for new model instances.
[02:52] [slight crosstalk]
[03:00] Jordan: on harness integration — can you describe your current client scripts and the format? are they node/python runners or custom SDK?
[03:08] Carlos: we have three flavors: electron desktop client, mobile iOS adapter, and a server-side python worker. they each emit slightly different framing. we can export sanitized scripts but timestamps and speaker-change boundaries are important to keep.
[03:20] Evan: perfect — we'll need a canonical harness adapter that accepts a short manifest (json) listing: session id, token arrival timestamps, speaker labels, and expected ground-truth segments. we'll provide an adapter template for node and python.
[03:34] Maya: telemetry hooks — we need to push traces back to our tracing stack (we use Datadog). are you able to emit span IDs or a correlation id?
[03:42] Priya: yes, the harness can attach correlation IDs and export metrics via statsd/exporter. we'll add a dd-trace shim in the example adapter.
[03:50] Tomoko: how do you handle streaming fallback? if the streaming model can't keep up, do you buffer and switch to non-stream? we don't want users to stare at a frozen spinner.
[03:58] Priya: Redwood can do dynamic routing — policy-based. we can define a latency gate: if p95 for last 1 min > 250ms, route new sessions to a lower-latency model variant or edge region; alternatively we can degrade to lower-quality but faster model. there's also a client-side backpressure option where the harness reduces transcript chunking.
[04:16] Carlos: cost-wise, what's the expected delta between streaming-optimized variant and batch-quantized?
[04:22] Evan: rough ballpark — streaming optimized (float16) vs batch 4-bit quantized could be 3x cost per token difference for long sequences, depends on batching. our Optimize tool will recommend quantization profile for batch jobs.
[04:34] Samir: we need explicit guardrails — e.g., a cost ceiling for the POC. we can't exceed $X/day.
[04:40] Jordan: we can model cost scenarios in the kickoff spreadsheet; priya will run a quick estimate for the expected token mix and traffic shape.
[04:48] [pause / typing sounds]
[04:55] Priya: quick note on measurement windows — for streaming we'll run steady-state windows of 30 minutes across 3 separate days during peak hours; for batch we'll run two full reprocess jobs and measure total wall time and per-token cost.
[05:10] Tomoko: that sounds fine. do you need synthetic users or will our recorded 48h trace suffice?
[05:18] Carlos: we can provide a 48h anonymized trace that has the real distribution. maybe add a synthetic noise generator to exercise bursts.
[05:26] Priya: yes please provide trace + three sanitized client scripts. we'll convert them to harness scenarios: 1) live small group (8-12 tokens/sec), 2) webinar high verbosity (40 tokens/sec burst), 3) batch backfill.
[05:38] Jordan: for acceptance, aside from latency and fidelity, we should also define reliability thresholds — e.g., <= 0.5% error rate (5xx or timeouts) during steady state.
[05:46] Maya: security check: audit logs must include request-level metadata for 90 days and SSO to our IDP (SAML).
[05:54] Jordan: noted — we'll include SAML and audit log options in the runbook. for the POC we can enable token-level logging with redaction.
[06:04] Evan: about telemetry — do you want token-level cost attribution? that helps you map feature usage to unit economics.
[06:12] Tomoko: yes, token attribution per session is important for PM metrics.
[06:16] Priya: we'll ensure the harness emits tokens-per-session and cost-per-session metrics; Redwood Console can display per-route totals.
[06:24] Carlos: what about KV cache behavior — our app has long-running sessions with context windows ~16k tokens; we care about cache hit rates to reduce repeated compute.
[06:34] Priya: our runtime supports prefix/KV caching; we'll instrument cache hit/miss and show how hit rate impacts latency and cost. for long contexts, the batch path with quantization is more cost effective after caching warmup.
[06:46] Samir: any special network requirements for streaming websockets vs http?
[06:52] Evan: streaming uses a websocket or HTTP/2 stream; we'll provide both adapter patterns. websockets give lower overhead for long-lived sessions.
[07:02] Tomoko: what about acceptance testing for regression on summarization quality — how will we measure?
[07:08] Priya: we'll run your suite of prompts against redwood models and your baseline and compute relative delta on ROUGE and a couple of human-labeled checks. we'll flag anything >3% regression. if we see regressions we can test alternative model variants or tune decoding parameters.
[07:20] Carlos: decoding parameters are important. Beam vs sampling differences. we want deterministic-ish outputs for downstream indexing.
[07:28] Priya: we'll lock sampling seeds in the harness for deterministic runs during benchmark windows.
[07:34] [brief overlap/indistinct]
[07:40] Jordan: timeline proposal: share runbook and adapter by 4/20, customer delivers scripts + traces by 4/22, kickoff the benchmark the week of 4/25 with an initial smoke test day 1 and 3 measurement days over week 1–2, review results and next steps end of week 2. total pilot ~3 weeks. good?
[07:58] Tomoko: that's aggressive but doable. we might need a legal/MRA review for VPC peering — that could add 5 business days.
[08:06] Maya: yes legal will review the peering. can you provide the minimum set of docs we need to start networking?
[08:12] Jordan: we'll attach a short SOC2 appendix, peering template, and KMS integration sheet in the runbook.
[08:20] Carlos: another question: do you support mixed-serving where we route short utterances to a small fast model and long context to a larger model? we want to avoid sending bulky context to the heavy model unnecessarily.
[08:30] Priya: yep — request classifiers / routing rules can be part of the harness. we can run a pre-filter that inspects session metadata and chooses route. we'll provide example rules.
[08:40] Evan: for the benchmark we'll include an ablation: all streaming to big model vs hybrid routing vs batch-only to show tradeoffs on cost/latency/fidelity.
[08:50] Tomoko: what constitutes pass/fail? if the hybrid meets p95 but fidelity drops 2.5% is that acceptable?
[08:58] Carlos: we discussed earlier: <=3% regression is acceptable. also cost per 1M tokens must be within our budget projection — we'll confirm the $ ceiling in the spreadsheet.
[09:08] Priya: noted. we'll produce a comparison table in the results: p95/p99, p50, error rate, cost per 1M, and cache hit rate.
[09:16] Samir: on credentials for the harness, can we use short-lived STS tokens or do you expect static API keys?
[09:24] Jordan: either, but for peering + private we prefer STS/assume-role patterns; we'll document both.
[09:30] Maya: if we do dedicated, can you expose metrics to our Grafana?
[09:36] Evan: yes, we can push to a Prometheus endpoint behind peering; we'll include a dashboard template.
[09:44] [background rustling]
[09:50] Tomoko: are there any gotchas with streaming tail latency? historically we've seen a long tail when KV cache misses cascade.
[09:58] Priya: right — we're planning cache warmup and synthetic warmup runs to prime KV. also we'll test cold-start scenarios where we can measure instance spin-up times.
[10:08] Carlos: how deterministic are your cold starts? we need numbers for SLA negotiation.
[10:14] Jordan: we'll include observed cold-start percentiles from our prior infra: typical spin-up ranges 600ms–3s depending on model size and region; we'll surface model-specific numbers in the runbook and in the benchmarks.
[10:28] Tomoko: ok. on the harness format, please define a canonical manifest schema. we want to make minimal changes to our apps.
[10:36] Priya: will do — the manifest will be a small json lines format: session_id, timestamp list, speaker_id, expected groundtruth, correlation_id. we'll provide conversion scripts for your three clients.
[10:46] Carlos: one more ask: can you run an early smoke with our mobile script only to validate real network conditions?
[10:52] Jordan: absolutely, we'll do a smoke test day 0 before the main measurement windows.
[11:00] Maya: legal wants to see data retention and purge flows. what logs do you keep?
[11:06] Jordan: for the POC we can keep request-level logs for 90 days; transcripts can be redacted on request. we'll include purge APIs in the runbook.
[11:14] Tomoko: okay great. anything else around evals?
[11:18] Priya: we'll run the human evaluation slice — 200 random segments — to validate ROUGE deltas and flag any qualitative issues.
[11:26] Carlos: process question: if results are good, what's the path to Dedicated or Private?
[11:32] Jordan: typical flow: pilot -> business review -> committed Dedicated contract or Private deployment. we can show cost models for both.
[11:40] Samir: timeline for Private is longer, right?
[11:44] Jordan: yes Private on-prem or VPC-based private control plane is 6–8 weeks post-contract; Dedicated is faster (2–3 weeks) depending on capacity.
[11:54] [short pause]
[12:00] Tomoko: recap then: runbook + adapters by 4/20, scripts & traces by 4/22, smoke test then measurement days week of 4/25, results review end of week 2. deliverables: runbook, harness adapter, cost spreadsheet, SOC2/peering appendix.
[12:18] Jordan: i'll email the runbook and a kickoff calendar invite. priya and evan will prep the adapter and dashboards.
[12:26] Carlos: we'll target to get artifacts to you by 4/22; legal will try to expedite peering.
[12:32] Tomoko: ok thanks everyone.
[12:36] Jordan: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
